2023 · NeurIPS 2023 · Benchmarks & Evals

ImageReward: Learning and Evaluating Human Preferences for Text-to-Image Generation

A 137k-comparison expert annotation pipeline (ImageRewardDB) trains a BLIP-backed preference scorer, ImageReward, that beats CLIP/Aesthetic/BLIP scores by 7–19 points across every column of its preference-accuracy evaluation — and ReFL, a fine-tuning method that back-propagates that scorer's gradient straight through a diffusion model's denoising chain, no reward-filtered dataset required.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By early 2023, text-to-image diffusion and autoregressive models were fast, popular, and still unreliable in ways that had nothing to do with resolution or FID: they mis-rendered counts, attributes and relationships in the prompt ("text-image alignment"), produced distorted or duplicated limbs ("body problem"), drifted from what people actually find pleasing ("human aesthetic"), and sometimes generated toxic or biased content. None of the standard automatic metrics were built to catch any of this. Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score are both batch-level statistics over the model's own output distribution (FID additionally compares that distribution to a set of real reference images) — neither says anything about whether an individual image matches its own prompt, and the paper argues zero-shot FID on MS-COCO is doubly suspect: many models may have seen COCO-like data during pre-training, and FID's whole-dataset averaging can't function as a per-image selector the way a user picking one output from a batch needs. CLIP score and BLIP score, the usual per-image alternative, measure text-image similarity only — not fidelity, not aesthetic quality, not harmlessness, and (as the paper later shows) not with much resolving power between similar-quality images.

The second half of the gap is about training, not evaluation. In NLP, RLHF has a well-established recipe: train a reward model on human preference comparisons, then use PPO to optimize a policy against it, relying on the policy's token-level likelihoods. Diffusion models have no such likelihood for a full generation — each image is the endpoint of a many-step denoising chain, not a single sampled sequence — so the standard RLHF machinery doesn't transfer. Classifier guidance is inference-only and requires training a classifier on noisy intermediate latents, which conflicts with how human raters actually judge images (only once fully denoised). The concurrent alternatives the paper compares against — filtering a fine-tuning dataset by reward score, or re-weighting a fine-tuning loss by reward — are indirect: they never put a reward gradient directly into the model's weights.

// how it works

The method

The paper is really two contributions built on one annotation effort. First comes ImageRewardDB: prompts are drawn from DiffusionDB (1.8M real user prompts), diversity-selected down to 10,000 via a graph-based algorithm over Sentence-BERT prompt embeddings (each prompt connected to its 150 nearest neighbors, then vertices selected repeatedly by a score the paper says is "related to the number of neighbors that have not yet been selected," without spelling out the exact scoring function). Each selected prompt keeps 4–9 sampled DiffusionDB images. Professional annotators — recruited through a data annotation company, most with at least college-level education — first label each prompt (category, ambiguity, latent toxicity), then rate every image on three 7-point Likert scales (overall, image-text alignment, fidelity) with binary problem checkboxes (body, toxicity, etc.), and finally rank all of a prompt's images into 5 preference slots (ties allowed). A written trade-off policy resolves the recurring conflict between "matches the prompt better" and "is more harmful/lower-fidelity": fidelity and harmlessness generally outrank alignment, except when an image is only slightly less faithful/harmless but clearly better aligned. After two months, this produced 8,878 valid prompts and 136,892 compared pairs — the paper rounds this to "137k" in its headline claim.

// version note

arXiv hosts four revisions of this paper; the text and figures on this page follow v4 (28 Dec 2023), the NeurIPS 2023 camera-ready — the version source ↗ resolves to at the top of the record. The original v1 preprint (12 Apr 2023), which is what many early citations quote, reports materially different numbers for large parts of the evaluation: its preference-accuracy, recall/filter, and FID/CLIP-alignment tables use a different, earlier snapshot of the annotation data and model checkpoints than the ones reproduced below. Every number on this page was checked against v4's own PDF text and cross-referenced against a 92-token list of values that appear in v1 but not in v4, specifically to avoid quoting a stale v1 figure that happens to look plausible.

ImageReward itself uses a BLIP backbone (the paper's own ablation shows BLIP beating CLIP at every matched training-set size — see below), extracting image and text features, combining them via cross-attention, and mapping to a scalar with an MLP head. Given a prompt T and a preferred/dispreferred image pair (xi, xj) drawn from the ranking data, the model is trained with a pairwise logistic loss:

loss(θ) = −𝔼(T,xᵢ,xⱼ)∼D[log(σ(fθ(T, xᵢ) − fθ(T, xⱼ)))] // f_θ(T, x): scalar preference score; xᵢ ranked above xⱼ for prompt T

Training is unstable without care: the paper reports rapid overfitting, addressed by freezing 70% of BLIP's transformer layers, and settles on a learning rate of 1e-5 with batch size 64 after a hyperparameter sweep.

The second contribution, ReFL (Reward Feedback Learning), solves the no-likelihood problem by exploiting an empirical property of the reward model rather than working around it. Scoring the partially-denoised latent at every step of a 40-step denoising schedule and asking whether the eventual image's quality is already visible in that intermediate prediction, the paper finds three regimes: through roughly step 15 of 40, ImageReward's score on the directly-predicted image is uniformly low and uninformative; between steps 15 and 30, high-quality generations begin to separate from the rest but not reliably; past step 30, scores become reliably distinguishable across seeds.

ReFL exploits exactly that window: for each training example it denoises a latent without gradient tracking down to a randomly sampled late step t, takes one further step with gradient tracking, predicts the final image directly from that single step (rather than iterating the rest of the way), scores the prediction with ImageReward, and back-propagates that reward as a loss — re-weighted (λ=1e-3, ϕ=ReLU) and mixed with the ordinary diffusion pre-training loss to keep the model from collapsing onto reward-hacking degenerate solutions. In the paper's own indexing (Algorithm 1), the sampled step t counts down from the end of the schedule (T=40) rather than up from the start, so the reported range [T₁,T₂]=[1,10] for t corresponds to the same late portion of the trajectory — roughly steps 30–39 of 40 already completed — that Figure 4 shows becoming score-distinguishable, not a contradiction between the two presentations, just two directions of the same clock. ReFL fine-tunes Stable Diffusion v1.4 on a 625k LAION-5B-aesthetic-filtered pre-training subset plus DiffusionDB-sampled prompts, 8 A100 GPUs, half precision, learning rate 1e-5, batch size 128 (64 pre-training + 64 ReFL) for one epoch.

// what they found

The results

On the model-ranking task (Table 1: six popular text-to-image models — Openjourney, Stable Diffusion 2.1-base and 1.4, DALL·E 2, Versatile Diffusion, CogView 2 — ranked by human annotators and by each automatic metric), ImageReward's ranking on real-user prompts matches the human ranking exactly, Spearman ρ = 1.00, versus CLIP score's ρ = 0.60 on the same prompts. Evaluated instead on MS-COCO 2014 (256×256, zero-shot), ImageReward still tracks human preference reasonably (ρ = 0.77) while zero-shot FID is nearly uncorrelated with it (ρ = 0.09) — the paper's headline argument that FID is the wrong tool for judging which model humans actually prefer.

On the model's core task — preference prediction on a held-out set of 466 prompts (6,399 comparison pairs) — ImageReward reaches 65.14% pairwise accuracy, ahead of BLIP score (57.76%), Aesthetic score (57.35%) and CLIP score (54.82%). On a separate best/worst-selection test (371 prompts, 8 images each), ImageReward also leads on every Recall@{1,2,4} and Filter@{1,2,4} metric — Recall@4 90.84% (runner-up: CLIP score, 78.17%) and Filter@4 88.95% (runner-up: BLIP score, 80.59%); the three baselines don't hold a consistent order column-to-column, only ImageReward's top spot is stable. Backbone matters: an ablation swapping BLIP for CLIP (same MLP head, same training recipe) tops out at 62.98% accuracy at 8k training prompts, below BLIP's 65.14% at the same data budget — and BLIP at its smallest tested size (1k prompts, 63.07%) already beats CLIP at its largest (8k, 62.98%), which is the paper's own point that a larger training set doesn't make up for CLIP's weaker backbone. ImageReward also visibly separates individual samples better than CLIP score — its per-model score distributions have much wider interquartile ranges (Figure 3) — which the paper argues matters for using a scorer as a single-image selector, not just a model-level ranker.

Used as a top-3 selector out of pools of 9, 25, and 64 candidate images, ImageReward beats random selection, CLIP score, Aesthetic score and BLIP score on every comparison in Figure 5 — averaging 77.1% win rate against random selection, 69.3% against CLIP, 69.8% against Aesthetic, and 65.8% against BLIP score across all three pool sizes.

For ReFL, human evaluation against the SD v1.4 baseline (Table 4) gives ReFL a 58.79% win rate on 466 real-user prompts and 58.49% on 90 MT-Bench prompts — the best of the four fine-tuning methods tested, ahead of Dataset Filtering (55.17% / 51.72%), RAFT at its first iteration (49.86% / 42.31%), and Reward Weighted (39.52% / 43.33%). RAFT's win rate strictly worsens across its own iterations (49.86% → 30.85% → 20.97% on real-user prompts), which the paper attributes to the fine-tuning dataset's expert-generator regularizer failing to keep pace as the reward-filtered training distribution narrows. A separate pairwise matrix (Figure 6) confirms the same pattern head-to-head: ReFL beats every other fine-tuning method it was compared against, with win rates ranging from 52% against Dataset Filtering (barely above a coin flip) up to 85% against three-iteration RAFT (which is, by that point, also the most degraded baseline in the comparison).

// does it hold up?

The eval read

Inside this paper's own tables, ImageReward's case is close to airtight: it wins all 21 baseline×column cells of Table 3 against CLIP/Aesthetic/BLIP score, by margins that range from 7.38 points (preference accuracy over BLIP score, the smallest gap anywhere in the table) to 19.41 points (Filter@1 over CLIP score, the largest), and ReFL beats every compared fine-tuning method in pairwise human evaluation. But two things narrow that story once you look outside this one paper's own protocol.

First, the margin over CLIP/Aesthetic/BLIP score is not the margin over the field. The paper's own Appendix D (Table 5) adds HPS and PickScore — the two other reward models published in the same few months — to the identical 466-prompt/371-prompt test protocol used for Table 3. Against these contemporaries, ImageReward's lead shrinks to single digits everywhere and reverses on one metric: HPS actually edges ImageReward on Recall@1 (39.89% vs. 39.62%), and PickScore ties ImageReward exactly on Recall@2 (63.07% vs. 63.07%). Counting every head-to-head cell — Table 5's 7 Recall/Filter/Acc. columns ×2 rivals (14 cells) plus Table 6's 4 Bo64/ReFL WinRate comparisons ×2 rivals (8 cells) — 22 comparisons in total — ImageReward wins 20, ties 1 (PickScore, Recall@2) and loses 1 (HPS, Recall@1); its margin over PickScore tops out around 7 points and over HPS around 8 — a different regime from the 7.4–19.4 point margins over the older embedding-similarity baselines in Table 3. The paper's framing ("ImageReward outperforms existing text-image scoring methods") is true, but it blends two very different comparison classes into one claim.

Second, and more consequential: independent tests by the authors of two concurrent papers, using their own held-out data, put real pressure on the headline number. Kirstain et al. (Pick-a-Pic) re-evaluate ImageReward on their own 500-example preference test set and get 61.1% accuracy — noticeably below the 65.14% this paper reports on its own test set — and, on a larger check correlating each scorer's Elo ratings against real users' Elo ratings over 14,000 preferences spanning 45 models, ImageReward's correlation (0.492 ± 0.086) is the weakest of the three preference-trained scorers tested — behind PickScore (0.790 ± 0.054) and HPS v1 (0.670 ± 0.071) — and ahead only of an off-the-shelf zero-shot CLIP-H baseline (0.313 ± 0.075), third of the four scorers overall. Wu et al. (HPS v2) run a more direct version of the same check: on ImageReward's own test set, ImageReward scores 65.1% — consistent with this paper's own number, and close behind only HPS v2 itself (65.7%). But evaluated instead on HPS v2's own broader test set — nine different generators plus real COCO photos, rather than the near-single-source pool ImageReward was trained and tested on — ImageReward's accuracy falls to 74.0%, second-worst of the six models Wu et al. compare: still ahead of zero-shot CLIP's 65.1%, but now trailing the Aesthetic Score Predictor's 76.8% (a baseline ImageReward's own Table 3 had beaten by 7.79 points on its home turf) and HPS v1's 77.6% (HPS doesn't appear in Table 3 at all — on the closest matching protocol, Table 5, ImageReward's edge over HPS was a much narrower 4.35 points). That is consistent with a real generalization gap rather than noise: ImageRewardDB's images come almost entirely from a narrow band of Stable-Diffusion-family and similar diffusion outputs sampled from DiffusionDB, so a scorer trained on it has limited exposure to other generator families' failure modes.

Table 6 has a sharper problem than a units mismatch. Its "Reward" column header is printed on two lines — "Image" above "Reward" — and reads as a single column, ImageReward, applied uniformly to every row: the SD v1.4 baseline row carries a value there too (0.1058 / 0.1859), which is only possible if the column is one fixed external scorer, since the baseline has no reward model of its own. That means the Bo64 and ReFL blocks, each built by selecting or fine-tuning against a specific reward model (HPS, PickScore, or ImageReward), are reported in a column that is ImageReward's own score — so the ImageReward-guided rows top that column in three of its four cells — overwhelmingly under Bo64, where the metric is the selection rule (1.3374 / 1.4098, roughly double PickScore’s 0.7033 / 0.7579 and HPS’s 0.6274 / 0.6788), and far more weakly under ReFL, where the optimization is indirect (0.6072 vs 0.4618 / 0.4749 on one benchmark, and actually losing on MT-Bench, 0.4822 against PickScore-tuned ReFL’s 0.4908): each row is graded, in that column, by the same metric only one of the three rows was optimized against. That is a textbook Goodhart setup, not evidence ImageReward is the better scorer, and the paper never flags it. The #Win/WinRate columns — independent human ranking — are the only honest cross-row comparison in that table.

On annotation methodology, the paper's own Limitations section is candid: each prompt is annotated by a single person rather than by multiple annotators reaching consensus — even though a separate quality inspector reviews every single annotation, not a sample of them, reassigning invalid ones for relabeling (§2.1) — and all prompts come from one source distribution (DiffusionDB) that the authors acknowledge carries its own biases relative to real-world usage beyond "trying strange prompts."

baselines

Fair and complete for its era against the field it names in the main results (CLIP score, Aesthetic score, BLIP score) — and the appendix goes further, adding the two genuinely contemporary reward models (HPS, PickScore) on the identical protocol. The gap between "beats old embedding-similarity metrics by a mile" and "beats other 2023 reward models by a few points, and loses one column to HPS" is real and is not foregrounded in the abstract or intro.

contamination

No leakage in the classic train/test sense — the 466-prompt test set is held out from the 8,878 annotated prompts. The more relevant risk is distributional: both training and test images are drawn almost entirely from DiffusionDB's Stable-Diffusion-family outputs, so in-paper numbers reflect performance on a near-single-generator-family test distribution, which independent cross-generator tests (HPS v2's HPD v2 test set) show does not transfer cleanly.

what's missed

How ImageReward behaves as a scorer for generator families it never saw during annotation — the in-paper evaluation never leaves the DiffusionDB/Stable-Diffusion-adjacent pool it was built from, so the sharpest evidence of its limits comes from two other groups' papers, not this one.

would raise confidence

A held-out test split built from generators absent from ImageRewardDB's training pool (GANs, autoregressive T2I models, later diffusion checkpoints), reported inside this paper rather than reconstructed after the fact by Pick-a-Pic and HPS v2; and a version of Table 3 that includes HPS/PickScore in the main text rather than relegated to an appendix table most readers won't reach.

// bottom line

The annotation pipeline and the ReFL training trick are the parts that hold up best: 136,892 rank-and-rate comparisons collected under an explicit, documented trade-off policy is a real methodological contribution, and back-propagating reward through a randomly-sampled late denoising step is a clean, well-motivated answer to "diffusion models have no likelihood." The scorer itself is genuinely strong on old-style metrics and genuinely competitive — not dominant — against its true 2023 peers, and two independent re-evaluations (Pick-a-Pic, HPS v2) each find it weaker once the test distribution moves even slightly away from DiffusionDB's Stable-Diffusion-heavy pool: a lower absolute accuracy on Pick-a-Pic's own test set (61.1% vs. this paper's 65.14%), and, on HPS v2's broader test set, a rank collapse rather than a lower number — 74.0% is numerically higher than 65.14%, but second-worst of six models instead of near-best.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. ImageReward pairs a documented 3-stage annotation pipeline (rate on alignment/fidelity/overall, then rank into 5 preference slots, with an explicit written trade-off policy for conflicting criteria) with a BLIP-backed pairwise reward model, reaching 65.14% preference accuracy and topping every Recall@{1,2,4}/Filter@{1,2,4} column against CLIP, Aesthetic and BLIP score baselines, over 136,892 expert comparisons on 8,878 DiffusionDB prompts.
  2. ReFL solves diffusion models' "no likelihood" problem empirically rather than architecturally: it exploits the finding that ImageReward's score on a directly-predicted image only becomes reliably informative in the last quarter of a 40-step denoising schedule, back-propagating a reward gradient from a randomly sampled step in that window — and it beats three indirect baselines (Dataset Filtering, Reward Weighted, RAFT) in every pairwise human comparison, from a 52% win rate against Dataset Filtering up to 85% against a fully-degraded RAFT checkpoint.
  3. The headline "outperforms existing text-image scoring methods" claim mixes two different comparison classes: a decisive 7.4–19.4-point win over older embedding-similarity metrics (CLIP/Aesthetic/BLIP score), and a much narrower, occasionally-losing 1–8-point contest against the two genuinely contemporary reward models (HPS, PickScore) — and independent re-tests by those same papers' authors, on their own data, put ImageReward's accuracy 4 points lower (61.1% on Pick-a-Pic's test set) and its cross-generator generalization near the bottom of the field (74.0% on HPS v2's nine-generator test set, versus a near-best 65.1% on its own single-source-heavy test set).
